Your First Motorcycle Tour: The Essential Checklist

There's nothing quite like the anticipation of your first motorcycle tour. The open road, the freedom, the wind in your... well, visor. But before you twist that throttle and head for the horizon, a bit of preparation goes a long way. We've put together the definitive checklist so you can focus on enjoying the ride rather than worrying about what you forgot.

Bike Preparation

Your motorcycle is your lifeline on tour. Give it the attention it deserves before departure day.

  • Oil and filter: Change your oil if you're within 500 miles of your next service interval. Fresh oil means a happy engine over long distances.
  • Chain tension and lubrication: A well-lubed chain with correct tension prevents breakdowns and improves fuel economy. Carry a can of chain lube with you.
  • Tyre condition and pressures: Check tread depth (minimum 1mm legal, but 2mm+ recommended for touring) and inflate to manufacturer specs for loaded riding.
  • Brake pads and fluid: Inspect pad thickness and top up brake fluid. Loaded touring puts extra demand on your brakes, especially in hilly terrain.
  • Coolant levels: Top up and check for leaks. Overheating in slow Highland traffic on a hot day is no joke.
  • Lights and electrics: Test every bulb, including brake lights and indicators. Carry spare bulbs — they weigh nothing.

Essential Documents

Getting stopped without paperwork is a fast way to ruin a tour. Keep these in a waterproof pouch:

  • Driving licence (full, with motorcycle entitlement)
  • Insurance certificate or digital proof
  • MOT certificate (if applicable)
  • Vehicle registration document (V5C)
  • Breakdown cover membership details
  • Ferry booking confirmations (printed backup)

Riding Gear Essentials

The UK weather is famously unpredictable. Layer up and prepare for everything from blazing sun to horizontal rain — sometimes in the same afternoon.

  • Waterproof jacket and trousers: Either dedicated waterproofs or a textile suit with a waterproof membrane. Test it before you go — some "waterproof" gear isn't.
  • Base layers: Merino wool is brilliant for temperature regulation. Pack at least two sets.
  • Gloves: Bring summer and waterproof winter gloves. Cold, wet hands destroy concentration.
  • Boots: Waterproof touring boots that you can walk in comfortably. You'll be off the bike as much as on it.
  • Neck tube or balaclava: Stops drafts and keeps you warm at altitude.

Navigation and Communication

Don't rely solely on your phone. Signal drops out across vast swathes of rural Britain, particularly in the Scottish Highlands, mid-Wales, and parts of Cumbria.

  • Download offline maps (OS Maps app is excellent for the UK)
  • Carry a physical road atlas as backup
  • Mount your phone securely — vibration can damage camera modules
  • Pack a USB power bank for emergency charging
  • Consider a Bluetooth intercom for group rides
Top tip: Test your entire setup — navigation, charging, luggage — on a day ride before committing to a multi-day tour. Better to discover problems 30 miles from home than 300.

Emergency and Comfort Kit

Hope for the best, prepare for the worst. A small emergency kit can save your tour:

  • Tyre repair kit and mini compressor
  • Basic tool roll (Allen keys, spanners, screwdrivers to fit your bike)
  • First aid kit
  • Torch (head torch is most practical)
  • Cable ties and gaffer tape — the motorcyclist's best friends
  • Sunscreen (yes, even in the UK — riding all day in summer sun burns)

Final Pre-Departure Checks

The night before you leave, run through this quick list:

  • Bike fuelled up and ready
  • Luggage packed and balanced (heavy items low and central)
  • Someone knows your rough itinerary and expected return
  • Phone fully charged, power bank topped up
  • Weather forecast checked for the first two days
  • Accommodation booked (or wild camping gear packed)

With this checklist ticked off, you're ready for the road. The first tour is always the most memorable — make it one to remember for all the right reasons. Read our Lightweight Summer Motorcycle Jackets for UK Touring guide for more.

faq.q: How far ahead should I service my bike before a first tour?
faq.a: Change your oil and filter if you are within 500 miles of your next service interval, and do it a week or two before departure rather than the night before. That gives you time to spot leaks or issues on a shakedown ride. Also check chain tension, tyre tread (2mm or more for touring), brake pads and coolant.

faq.q: What documents must I carry on a UK tour?
faq.a: Carry your full driving licence with motorcycle entitlement, insurance certificate or digital proof, MOT certificate if applicable, the V5C registration document and your breakdown cover membership details. Keep printed backups of any ferry confirmations. Store everything in a waterproof pouch, as wet paperwork is useless at a roadside check.

faq.q: Can I rely on my phone for navigation?
faq.a: Not entirely. Mobile signal disappears across large parts of the Scottish Highlands, mid-Wales and Cumbria. Download offline maps using the OS Maps app, mount your phone on a vibration-dampening cradle, and carry a physical road atlas as backup. Pack a power bank so a flat battery never leaves you stranded.

faq.q: How should I load luggage for stable handling?
faq.a: Put heavy items low and close to the bike's centre of gravity, and balance weight evenly side to side. A top-heavy tail bag makes the bike feel unstable through corners. Do not overload a tank bag to the point it blocks your view of the instruments, and test-ride the loaded bike before you set off.

faq.q: What is the single best pre-tour tip?
faq.a: Test everything on a day ride first. Load the bike exactly as you would for the tour, run your navigation and charging setup, and ride a full day. It is far better to discover a leaking pannier or a mount that vibrates loose 30 miles from home than 300 miles into a remote tour.
